1	---
2	name: horizon-start
3	description: Work out which situation you were launched into — first round of a fresh run, a hand-off from the horizon session that just finished, a resume after a crash or pause, or a session outside any run — and pull exactly the context that situation calls for. Load at the START of a session, before picking up the task.
4	---
5	
6	Your prompt carries the task and nothing else: no history, no word about who ran
7	before you or how they ended. That is deliberate — state is pulled, not pushed
8	(the `horizon` skill's stance). But it means a session that starts working
9	immediately is guessing. Usually somebody *was* here before you, often minutes
10	ago, and their report was written for you.
11	
12	This skill is the first pass: four cheap reads, a guess at the situation, then
13	the context that situation actually calls for. Budget a couple of minutes, not a
14	tenth of the session.
15	
16	## The four signals
17	
18	```bash
19	ls "$ARCHON_HORIZON_SESSION_DIR/.."     # sibling sessions in THIS run
20	"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json             # `paused` (why the last run stopped) + `recent_failure_reasons`
21	"$HORIZON_BIN" ps                       # is another run live on this workspace RIGHT NOW?
22	"$HORIZON_GIT" log --oneline -15        # what actually landed recently
23	```
24	
25	The sibling listing is the one that decides most of it. A run's sessions look
26	like:
27	
28	```
29	0001-system            ← orchestrator bookkeeping (commits, integration), not an agent
30	0002-horizon-PET.5     ← a horizon session; meta.json + transcript.jsonl + usage.json
31	0003-system
32	0004-horizon-PET.5     ← ...you, probably
33	```
34	
35	For any earlier `*-horizon-*` sibling, two files answer everything:
36	
37	- **`report.md` present** → that session finished on its own terms and wrote you
38	  a hand-off. **`report.md` absent** → it was killed mid-flight. This is the
39	  single most informative bit on disk.
40	- **`meta.json`** → `round`, `task_id`, `status`, `started_at`, `ended_at`,
41	  `model`. `ended_at` against the current time tells you whether "recent" means
42	  four minutes ago or last week.
43	
44	## Which situation am I in?
45	
46	Work down the list; the first match is your best guess.
47	
48	**An earlier horizon sibling has no `report.md`** → *resume after a crash or
49	kill.* Its work is half-done and possibly half-committed. Read its commits in
50	the ledger first (they are the part that survived), then the tail of its
51	transcript to see what it was in the middle of — `usage --json` `paused` gives
52	the reason it died (usage limit, budget, auth), and `recent_failure_reasons`
53	shows rate-limit pressure that may still be there. Trust the ledger over the
54	transcript: anything it did not commit is gone, no matter what it said it was
55	doing. If the dead session shares your `ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK`, you are continuing
56	its exact work — pick up its front rather than opening a new one.
57	
58	**An earlier horizon sibling has a `report.md`** → *hand-off from the session
59	that just finished.* The common case. Read that report first — its `## Next` and
60	`## Why I stopped` were written for exactly this moment — then its commits, then
61	any inbox items addressed to horizon since its `ended_at`. Do not re-derive what
62	it already established; do not redo a piece it says is done without checking the
63	ledger.
64	
65	**`ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUND` is `0` and no horizon sibling exists** → *first agent
66	of the run.* Nobody handed you anything **in this run** — but the workspace is
67	almost never greenfield. Earlier runs live under `.archon-horizon/runs/`; the
68	roadmap, the inbox and the ledger carry their conclusions. Skim the roadmap and
69	recent ledger history before deciding a strategy that a previous run already
70	tried and rejected.
71	
72	**`ARCHON_HORIZON_RUN` is unset** → *not launched by the orchestrator* (an
73	interactive or hand-driven session). No run context exists to reconstruct;
74	orient from workspace state — roadmap, inbox, ledger — and say where things
75	stand before proposing work.
76	
77	One caveat about round numbers. `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUND` is 0-based and reliable
78	for "am I first" — but a resumed run can re-run a round whose session died, so a
79	`0` with a dead sibling present means *resume*, not *fresh*. The dead-sibling
80	check settles it either way. (`ROUND + 1 == ROUNDS` is a sound last-round test,
81	resumed runs included — `ROUNDS` bounds the rounds *this* invocation drives, not
82	the run's original plan.)
83	
84	## Then, before you start
85	
86	- **`horizon ps` said another run is live?** You share one ledger branch with it.
87	  Commit in small coherent pieces and expect to see its commits interleaved.
88	- **Timestamps are context.** A predecessor that ended 90 seconds ago probably
89	  left a warm build; one that ended last week may have left a workspace that no
90	  longer compiles. Check rather than assume.
91	- **The inbox is the cross-session thread** — read what past sessions left for
92	  horizon, and the task's own comments if you share their `task_id`
93	  (`"$HORIZON_BIN" task show "$ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK" --json`). Skill:
94	  `horizon-inbox`.
95	
96	Then stop orienting and start working. The point of this pass is to begin from a
97	smarter place than round zero — not to reconstruct everything that ever happened
98	here.
99

input.command: cd "$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT"; ls "$ARCHON_HORIZON_SESSION_DIR/.."; echo "---USAGE"; "$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json 2>/dev/null | head -60; echo "---PS"; "$HORIZON_BIN" ps 2>&1 | head -30; echo "---LOG"; "$HORIZON_GIT" log --oneline -20

=== REPORT
All six commits are in the ledger and the workspace is hand-off clean. The three helpers I dispatched never returned reports, so the required fresh-context review did not happen — I'll say that plainly in the report rather than imply the work was independently audited.

## Summary

Advanced three of the four fronts of the A.3 leg with real, kernel-checked content, and corrected the roadmap where it described the remaining work wrongly. The headline: `smooth` and `proper` are no longer open obligations but assemblies over one named input each, and that "one input is the whole residue" claim is *measured* (axiom probe with a control), not argued. Sorry counts are unchanged (3/3/1) — what changed is what the sorries are.

## Progress

- `Picard/Pic0AbelianVariety.lean`: 3 sorries → 3, each strictly smaller. `smooth` = `smooth_of_geometricallyReduced` (**proved**, from mathlib's `smooth_of_grpObj`, which already contains the translation argument *and* the descent along `Spec k̄ → Spec k`) + `geometricallyReduced` (the sole residue: Cartier in char 0, `H²(C,𝒪_C)=0` in char p). `proper` = `proper_of_universallyClosed` (**proved**: `IsProper` is three fields, and this file had already proved separatedness and finite-type — they were sitting unused beside the sorry) + `universallyClosed`. `finrank_cotangentSpaceDual_eq_finrank_h1Cok` **is no longer a sorry**, proved from one named geometric input via a new sorry-free general lemma `finrank_eq_of_addEquiv_of_bijective_smul` (the `finrank` form of `rank_eq_of_equiv_equiv` — the right instrument because the two sides live over *different* rings, κ(e) and k, so `LinearEquiv.finrank_eq` and `restrictScalars` both fail).
- `Picard/IdentityComponent.lean`: 3 sorries → 3, plus new sorry-free `Pic0Scheme.inclusion`. Split the closed half out of `kPoints_iff_kerDegree`; located the real blocker of `finrank_eq_genus` — a **missing mathlib bridge** from `topologicalKrullDim` to relative dimension, not the tangent identity.
- `RiemannRoch/WeilDivisor.lean`: 1 sorry → 1, deliberately. Documented two independent obstructions the roadmap omitted.

## Issues

- **The roadmap was wrong about `AJC.rr.principal`.** It claimed the residue was "ONE input, a one-point local statement". In fact (i) the adelic endpoint is *downstream* of `WeilDivisor.lean`, so substituting it is an import inversion, and (ii) the bump route is refuted in-tree by `ChiUnconditional.not_bump_of_notMem_left`. I also recorded why that refutation is *not* fatal — its `Module.Finite` chart-section binder is a substantive restriction excluding the curves Riemann–Roch is about — so the open work is exhibiting a usable cover. Node rewritten.
- **`PicScheme.degree`: no route found I would stand behind.** Its intended construction runs through Quot, which is retained-not-revived. I did not give it a definition that merely typechecks, since `kPoints_iff_kerDegree` and the Albanese lane consume its *value*.
- **`scripts/axiom-frontier.lean` consumes the false leaf** that protection I-0491 orders deleted (`:358`, `:433`). Flagged to ajc-etale-pic rather than touching their files; the project's own axiom instrument will stop compiling when the leaf goes.
- **The three subagents I dispatched (work-reviewer, janitor, degree-map scout) never returned reports** — their transcripts went quiet at stub size. So the required fresh-context review of this diff did **not** happen. My claims rest on my own kernel build and axiom probe, not on independent audit.

## Why I stopped

Partly advanced, not complete — so I set no terminal status and the task returns to the queue. Three of four fronts moved; none of the four closed. Two are blocked on things I could not honestly resolve (the degree map, and the missing Krull-dimension bridge), and the tangent lane's residue is now a single geometric statement that is genuine multi-session work. Everything is committed (six commits) and `lake build` of all three edited modules completes successfully with zero errors.

## Next

1. `geometricallyReduced` and `universallyClosed` are now the two cheapest real wins in this lane — each is one theorem, with sources and the circularity trap documented at the site.
2. For the tangent lane, the residue needs no Hilbert 90 and no henselian machinery (confirmed from the AJCR side): the thickening is square-zero, so `Algebra.FormallyEtale.comp_bijective` covers it.
3. `finrank_eq_genus` needs the Kähler-differentials rank bridge, or consumers should retarget to `SmoothOfRelativeDimension (genus C)`.
4. Someone should re-run the fresh-context review that did not land here.

CROSS-PROJECT THREAD — AJC and AJCR are doing the same mathematics twice; this is where you stop that

Eight teams launched on 2026-07-28, four on Algebraic-Jacobian-Challenge and four on Algebraic-Jacobian-Challenge-Rebuild. The two projects overlap heavily and the workspace exists so the same lemma is not derived twice. This thread is for cross-project leads ONLY — per-project coordination goes on your own project thread.

THREE OVERLAPS ALREADY IDENTIFIED, with the evidence:

 1. THE ETALE-PLUS PICARD FUNCTOR. AJCR has it BUILT AND SORRY-FREE: Picard/PicEtAff.lean (394 lines), Picard/Pic0Functor.lean (182), Picard/RelPicCoverInjective.lean (89) — I re-verified zero sorries on 2026-07-28. AJC is about to need exactly this, because the human decision of today (protection I-0491) makes the etale-sheafified functor its representability target. ajc-etale-pic: read those three files BEFORE writing anything, then post here what you are porting, importing, or re-deriving and why. AJCR teams: correct them if they are about to reinvent something you have.

 2. dim T_0(Pic^0) = g, THE TANGENT/H1 COMPARISON. Being worked from BOTH sides simultaneously: ajc-pic0av on Picard/Pic0AbelianVariety.lean (tangentSpaceCotangentDual, finrank_cotangentSpaceDual_eq_finrank_h1Cok) and ajcr-w5-av on the T1/T3/T4/T5 chain. Two independent derivations of the same scalar identity is precisely the waste to avoid. Compare approaches here early. AJCRs T4 carries a real risk (the etale-plus / Zariski kernel crossing at k[epsilon]) that AJC may not face in the same form, or may face worse — that comparison is worth a post on its own.

 3. THE RIEMANN-ROCH / CLUSTER-P SUBSTRATE. AJCR has a 63-file, 17.8k-line RiemannRoch/ directory that is largely sorry-free and is essentially the cluster-P substrate AJC lacks. A predecessor assessment judged that auditing it for portability decides where the next two months go, more than any single proof would. /-

module

public import Mathlib.AlgebraicGeometry.AlgClosed.Basic
public import Mathlib.AlgebraicGeometry.Morphisms.LocalFlatDescent
public import Mathlib.AlgebraicGeometry.Geometrically.Reduced
public import Mathlib.CategoryTheory.Monoidal.Grp

/-!
# Smoothness of group schemes

## Main results
- `AlgebraicGeometry.smooth_of_grpObj`:
  If `G` is a group scheme over a field `k` that is geometrically reduced and locally
  of finite type, then `G` is smooth over `k`.
-/

public section

open CategoryTheory

namespace AlgebraicGeometry

universe u

variable {K : Type u} [Field K] {G : Scheme} (f : G ⟶ Spec (.of K))
    [LocallyOfFiniteType f] [GrpObj (Over.mk f)]

set_option backward.defeqAttrib.useBackward true in
set_option backward.isDefEq.respectTransparency false in
open MonObj MonoidalCategory CartesianMonoidalCategory in
/--
If `G` is a group scheme over an algebraically closed field `k` that is reduced and locally
of finite type, then `G` is smooth over `k`.
-/
private lemma smooth_of_grpObj_of_isAlgClosed [IsReduced G] [IsAlgClosed K] : Smooth f := by
  have := LocallyOfFiniteType.jacobsonSpace f
  have : Nonempty G := ⟨η[Over.mk f].1 (IsLocalRing.closedPoint _)⟩
  rw [← Scheme.Hom.smoothLocus_eq_top_iff, ← TopologicalSpace.Opens.coe_eq_univ,
    ← not_ne_iff, ← Set.nonempty_compl]
  intro H
  obtain ⟨x, hx, hxc⟩ :=
    nonempty_inter_closedPoints H f.smoothLocus.2.isClosed_compl.isLocallyClosed
  obtain ⟨y, hy : y ∈ f.smoothLocus, hyc⟩ := nonempty_inter_closedPoints
    f.dense_smoothLocus_of_perfectField.nonempty f.smoothLocus.2.isLocallyClosed
  let x' : 𝟙_ _ ⟶ Over.mk f := Over.homMk _ ((pointEquivClosedPoint f).symm ⟨x, hxc⟩).2
  let y' : 𝟙_ _ ⟶ Over.mk f := Over.homMk _ ((pointEquivClosedPoint f).symm ⟨y, hyc⟩).2
  let α := (GrpObj.mulRight (A := Over.mk f) x').symm ≪≫
    (GrpObj.mulRight (A := Over.mk f) y')
  have hα : x' ≫ α.hom = y' := by
    dsimp only [Iso.trans_hom, Iso.symm_hom, α]
    rw [← Category.assoc, ← Iso.eq_comp_inv]
    simp [comp_lift_assoc]
  have hα' : α.hom.left x = y := by
    simpa [x', y', pointEquivClosedPoint] using congr(($hα).left (IsLocalRing.closedPoint K))
  rw! [← hα', ← α.hom.left.mem_preimage, Scheme.Hom.preimage_smoothLocus_eq,
    show α.hom.left ≫ f = f from α.hom.w] at hy
  exact hx hy

lemma smooth_of_grpObj [GeometricallyReduced f] : Smooth f := by
  let Ω : Type u := AlgebraicClosure K
  let g : Spec (.of Ω) ⟶ Spec (.of K) := Spec.map (CommRingCat.ofHom <| algebraMap K Ω)
  apply MorphismProperty.of_pullback_snd_of_descendsAlong
    (Q := @Surjective ⊓ @Flat ⊓ @QuasiCompact) (g := g)
  · exact ⟨⟨inferInstance, inferInstance⟩, inferInstance⟩
  · let : GrpObj (Over.mk (Limits.pullback.snd f g)) := Over.grpObjMkPullbackSnd
    exact smooth_of_grpObj_of_isAlgClosed _

end AlgebraicGeometry

bijective := by

    apply LinearEquiv.bijective

protected theorem left : Module.Invertible R M := .right (TensorProduct.comm R N M ≪≫ₗ e)

instance : Module.Invertible R R := .left (TensorProduct.lid R R)

end LinearEquiv

variable [Module.Invertible R M]

protected theorem congr (e : M ≃ₗ[R] N) : Module.Invertible R N :=
  .right (e.symm.lTensor _ ≪≫ₗ linearEquiv R M)

variable (R M N)

instance : Module.Invertible R (Dual R M) := .left (linearEquiv R M)

instance [Module.Invertible R N] : Module.Invertible R (M ⊗[R] N) :=
  .right (M := Dual R M ⊗[R] Dual R N) <| tensorTensorTensorComm .. ≪≫ₗ
    congr (linearEquiv R M) (linearEquiv R N) ≪≫ₗ TensorProduct.lid R R

private theorem finite_projective : Module.Finite R M ∧ Projective R M := by
  let N := Dual R M
  let e : M ⊗[R] N ≃ₗ[R] R := TensorProduct.comm .. ≪≫ₗ linearEquiv R M
  have ⟨S, hS⟩ := TensorProduct.exists_finset (e.symm 1)
  let f : (S →₀ N) →ₗ[R] R := Finsupp.lsum R fun i ↦ e.toLinearMap ∘ₗ TensorProduct.mk R M N i.1.1
  have : Function.Surjective f := by
    rw [← LinearMap.range_eq_top, Ideal.eq_top_iff_one]
    use Finsupp.equivFunOnFinite.symm fun i ↦ i.1.2
    simp_rw [f, Finsupp.coe_lsum]
    rw [Finsupp.sum_fintype _ _ fun _ ↦ map_zero _]
    rwa [e.symm_apply_eq, map_sum, ← Finset.sum_coe_sort, eq_comm] at hS
  have ⟨g, hg⟩ := projective_lifting_property f .id this
  classical
  let aux := finsuppRight R _ M N S ≪≫ₗ Finsupp.mapRange.linearEquiv e
  let f' : (S →₀ R) →ₗ[R] M := TensorProduct.rid R M ∘ₗ f.lTensor M ∘ₗ aux.symm
  let g' : M →ₗ[R] S →₀ R := aux ∘ₗ g.lTensor M ∘ₗ (TensorProduct.rid R M).symm
  have : Function.Surjective f' := by simpa [f'] using LinearMap.lTensor_surjective _ this
  refine ⟨.of_surjective f' this, .of_split g' f' <| LinearMap.ext fun m ↦ ?_⟩
  simp [f', g', show f (g 1) = 1 from DFunLike.congr_fun hg 1]

instance : Module.Finite R M := (finite_projective R M).1
instance : Projective R M := (finite_projective R M).2
example : IsReflexive R M := inferInstance

section inj_surj_bij

variable {R N P}
end inj_surj_bij

open Finsupp in
variable {R M} in
/-- An invertible module is free iff it is isomorphic to the ring, i.e. its class is trivial in
the Picard group. -/
theorem free_iff_linearEquiv : Free R M ↔ Nonempty (M ≃ₗ[R] R) := by
  refine ⟨fun _ ↦ ?_, fun ⟨e⟩ ↦ .of_equiv e.symm⟩
  nontriviality R
  have e := (Free.chooseBasis R M).repr
  have := card_eq_of_linearEquiv R <|
    (finsuppTensorFinsupp' .. ≪≫ₗ linearEquivFunOnFinite R R _).symm ≪≫ₗ TensorProduct.congr
      (linearEquivFunOnFinite R R _ ≪≫ₗ llift R R R _ ≪≫ₗ e.dualMap)
      e.symm ≪≫ₗ linearEquiv R M ≪≫ₗ (.symm <| .funUnique Unit R R)
  have : Unique (Free.ChooseBasisIndex R M) :=
    (Fintype.card_eq_one_iff_nonempty_unique.mp (by simpa using this)).some
  exact ⟨e ≪≫ₗ uniqueLinearEquiv R R default⟩

protected theorem finrank_eq_one [Free R M] : finrank R M = 1 := by
  rw [(free_iff_linearEquiv.mp ‹_›).some.finrank_eq, CommSemiring.finrank_self]

theorem rank_eq_one [Free R M] : Module.rank R M = 1 :=
  rank_eq_one_iff_finrank_eq_one.mpr (Invertible.finrank_eq_one R M)

open TensorProduct (comm lid) in
theorem toModuleEnd_bijective : Function.Bijective (toModuleEnd R (S := R) M) := by
  have : toModuleEnd R (S := R) M = (lid R M).conj ∘ rTensorEquiv R R
      (comm .. ≪≫ₗ linearEquiv R M) ∘ RingEquiv.moduleEndSelf R ∘ MulOpposite.opEquiv := by
    ext; simp [LinearEquiv.conj, liftAux]
  simpa [this] using MulOpposite.opEquiv.bijective

instance : FaithfulSMul R M where
  eq_of_smul_eq_smul {_ _} h := (toModuleEnd_bijective R M).injective <| LinearMap.ext h

variable {R M N} in
private theorem bijective_self_of_surjective (f : R →ₗ[R] M) (hf : Function.Surjective f) :
    Function.Bijective f where
  left {r₁ r₂} eq := smul_left_injective' (α := M) <| funext fun m ↦ by
    obtain ⟨r, rfl⟩ := hf m
    simp_rw [← map_smul, smul_eq_mul, mul_comm _ r, ← smul_eq_mul, map_smul, eq]
  right := hf

variable {R M N} in
/- Not true if `surjective` is replaced by `injective`: any nonzero element in an invertible
module over a domain generates a submodule isomorphic to the domain, which is not the whole
module unless the module is free. -/
theorem bijective_of_surjective [Module.Invertible R N] {f : M →ₗ[R] N}
    (hf : Function.Surjective f) : Function.Bijective f := by
  simpa [lTensor_bijective_iff] using bijective_self_of_surjective
    (f.lTensor _ ∘ₗ (linearEquiv R M).symm.toLinearMap) (by simpa [lTensor_surjective_iff] using hf)

section LinearEquiv
variable {R M N} [Module.Invertible R N] {f : M →ₗ[R] N} {g : N →ₗ[R] M}

theorem rightInverse_of_leftInverse (hfg : Function.LeftInverse f g) :
    Function.RightInverse f g :=
  Function.rightInverse_of_injective_of_leftInverse
    (bijective_of_surjective hfg.surjective).injective hfg

theorem leftInverse_of_rightInverse (hfg : Function.RightInverse f g) :
    Function.LeftInverse f g :=
  rightInverse_of_leftInverse hfg

variable (f g) in
theorem leftInverse_iff_rightInverse :

/-!
# Geometrically Reduced Schemes

## Main results
- `AlgebraicGeometry.GeometricallyReduced`:
  We say that morphism `f : X ⟶ Y` is geometrically reduced if for all `Spec K ⟶ Y` with `K`
  a field, `X ×[Y] Spec K` is reduced.
  We also provide the fact that this is stable under base change (by `infer_instance`)
- `GeometricallyReduced.iff_geometricallyReduced_fiber`:
  A scheme is geometrically reduced over `S` iff the fibers of all
  `s : S` are geometrically reduced.
- `AlgebraicGeometry.GeometricallyReduced.isReduced_of_flat_of_isLocallyNoetherian`:
  If `X` is geometrically reduced and flat over a reduced and locally noetherian scheme,
  then `X` is also reduced.
  In particular, the base change of a geometrically reduced and flat scheme to an
  reduced and locally noetherian scheme is reduced (by `infer_instance`).

## TODO
Get rid of the noetherian assumption.
-/

variable {X Y Z S : Scheme} (f : X ⟶ S) (g : Y ⟶ S)

/-- We say that morphism `f : X ⟶ Y` is geometrically reduced if for all `Spec K ⟶ Y` with `K`
a field, `X ×[Y] Spec K` is reduced. -/
@[mk_iff]
class GeometricallyReduced (f : X ⟶ Y) : Prop where
  geometrically_isReduced : geometrically IsReduced f

lemma GeometricallyReduced.eq_geometrically :
    @GeometricallyReduced = geometrically IsReduced := by
  ext; exact geometricallyReduced_iff _

instance : IsStableUnderBaseChange @GeometricallyReduced :=
  GeometricallyReduced.eq_geometrically ▸ inferInstance

instance [GeometricallyReduced g] : GeometricallyReduced (pullback.fst f g) :=
  MorphismProperty.pullback_fst f g inferInstance

instance [GeometricallyReduced f] : GeometricallyReduced (pullback.snd f g) :=
  MorphismProperty.pullback_snd f g inferInstance

instance (V : S.Opens) [GeometricallyReduced f] : GeometricallyReduced (f ∣_ V) :=
  MorphismProperty.of_isPullback (isPullback_morphismRestrict ..).flip ‹_›

instance (s : S) [GeometricallyReduced f] :
    GeometricallyReduced (f.fiberToSpecResidueField s) :=
  MorphismProperty.pullback_snd _ _ inferInstance

instance (s : S) [GeometricallyReduced f] : IsReduced (f.fiber s) :=
  GeometricallyReduced.geometrically_isReduced _ _ _ (.of_hasPullback _ _)

  let g : Z ⟶ Y := Sigma.desc fun Z ↦ Y.fromSpecStalk _

  have : QuasiCompact g := ⟨fun _ _ _ ↦ (Set.toFinite _).isCompact⟩
  have H : IsSchemeTheoreticallyDominant g := by
    rw [isSchemeTheoreticallyDominant_iff_isDominant, isDominant_iff, denseRange_iff_closure_range,
      Set.eq_univ_iff_forall]
    intro y
    let z : Z := Sigma.ι (fun Z ↦ Spec (pt Z)) ⟨_, irreducibleComponent_mem_irreducibleComponents y⟩

        Scheme.fromSpecStalk_closedPoint]
      exact (IsIrreducible.isGenericPoint_genericPoint _

  have H := IsUniversalColimit.isPullback_of_isColimit_left
    (X := fun Z ↦ Spec (pt Z))
    (FinitaryPreExtensive.isUniversal_finiteCoproducts (coproductIsCoproduct _))
    (fun Z ↦ Y.fromSpecStalk _) g f _ _ (fun _ ↦ .of_hasPullback _ _) (coproductIsCoproduct _)

lemma GeometricallyReduced.isReduced_of_flat_of_isLocallyNoetherian
    (f : X ⟶ Y) [GeometricallyReduced f] [Flat f]
    [IsReduced Y] [IsLocallyNoetherian Y] : IsReduced X := by

    exact TopologicalSpace.NoetherianSpace.finite_irreducibleComponents

import AlgebraicJacobian.Picard.DivisorClassCompat
import AlgebraicJacobian.RiemannRoch.ChiCurve

/-!
# The degree homomorphism on the Čech Picard group

For the curve bundle `X` (integral, smooth of relative dimension one and quasi-compact over
a field `K`, with finite `H⁰`/`H¹` of the structure sheaf — the two instance hypotheses
through which properness enters), this file builds the **degree homomorphism** on the Čech
Picard group and records the E-i..E-iii interface of the degree lane
(`informal/degree-pic0-recon.md` §3 G-D3, `informal/deg-d2-meromorphic-worksheet.md` W5).

The anchored class map `CurveDivisor.picClass K : X.CurveDivisor → X.CechPic` of the
meromorphic bridge (`Picard/DivisorClassMeromorphic.lean`) is surjective, with fibres the
principal divisors. The degree of a Weil divisor is class-invariant: two divisors of equal
class differ by a principal divisor (extraction `(X)`, `CurveDivisor.exists_divOf_of_picClass_eq`)
and principal divisors have degree zero (`deg_divOf`, the χ-ledger), so `deg` descends to a
homomorphism on classes.

## Main declarations

* `AlgebraicGeometry.classDeg` — the degree homomorphism `Additive X.CechPic →+ ℤ`:
  `classDeg 𝒪(D) = deg D` for any Weil divisor `D`. The carrier `Additive X.CechPic →+ ℤ`
  is chosen so that a *value* `classDeg L` is a genuine integer: `X.CechPic` is a `CommGroup`
  (line-bundle tensor) and the degrees form the additive group `ℤ`, so the idiomatic
  packaging of "a group homomorphism from the multiplicative Picard group to the additive
  group `ℤ`" is an `AddMonoidHom` out of `Additive X.CechPic`. Because `Additive X.CechPic`
  is definitionally `X.CechPic`, the interface statements below read literally, and
  `map_zero`/`map_add`/`map_neg`/`map_zsmul` come for free from the bundled hom.
* `AlgebraicGeometry.classDeg_picClass` (**E-i**, normalization): `classDeg 𝒪(D) = deg D`,
  the definitional anchor, for *every* Weil divisor `D`.
* `AlgebraicGeometry.classDeg_mul` (**E-ii**, homomorphism):
  `classDeg (L · L') = classDeg L + classDeg L'`.
* `AlgebraicGeometry.chi_divisorSheaf_classDeg` (**E-iii**, χ-connection):
  `χ(𝒪(D)) = χ(𝒪_X) + classDeg 𝒪(D)`.
* `AlgebraicGeometry.chi_divisorSheaf_eq_of_picClass_eq`: the Euler characteristic of a class
  is well-defined — `𝒪(D) = 𝒪(D') → χ(𝒪(D)) = χ(𝒪(D'))` — via the multiplication
  isomorphism `mulEquivDivisorSheaf` and `chi_congr` (no finiteness needed).
* `AlgebraicGeometry.classDeg_divisorClass`: the deg-D1 divisor class map has the same degree,
  `classDeg (divisorClass K D) = deg D`, through the collapse `divisorClass_eq_picClass`.
* `AlgebraicGeometry.chi_divisorSheaf_classDeg_curve`: the curve form
  `χ(𝒪(D)) = 1 − genus C + classDeg 𝒪(D)` on the challenge curve.

The recon's E-i pushforward-rank reading (`classDeg 𝒪(D) = dim_K Γ(𝒪_D)` for *effective*
`D`, the Dedekind colength of the structure sheaf of the subscheme `D`) is a separate
statement about global sections of `𝒪_D`; it is *not* this brick's definitional anchor
(`classDeg 𝒪(D) = deg D`) and is deferred to a later node.
-/

set_option autoImplicit false

universe u

open CategoryTheory Limits Opposite

namespace AlgebraicGeometry

open Scheme

variable (K : Type u) [Field K] {X : Scheme.{u}} [X.Over (Spec (CommRingCat.of K))]
  [SmoothOfRelativeDimension 1 (X ↘ Spec (CommRingCat.of K))] [IsIntegral X]
  [QuasiCompact (X ↘ Spec (CommRingCat.of K))]
  [Module.Finite K (Sheaf.HModule (X.moduleKSheaf K) 0)]
  [Module.Finite K (Sheaf.HModule (X.moduleKSheaf K) 1)]

/-! ## χ of a class is well-defined (no finiteness hypotheses) -/

omit [Module.Finite K (Sheaf.HModule (X.moduleKSheaf K) 0)]
  [Module.Finite K (Sheaf.HModule (X.moduleKSheaf K) 1)] in
/-- **The Euler characteristic of a Čech Picard class is well-defined**: Weil divisors of
equal class have the same `χ(𝒪(D))`. If `𝒪(D) = 𝒪(D')` then `D − D' = div g` for a rational
function `g` (extraction `(X)`), and multiplication by `g` is an isomorphism of divisor
sheaves `𝒪(D) ≅ 𝒪(D − div g) = 𝒪(D')` (`mulEquivDivisorSheaf`), so the Euler
characteristics agree by `chi_congr`. Needs no finiteness hypotheses. -/
theorem chi_divisorSheaf_eq_of_picClass_eq {D D' : X.CurveDivisor}
    (h : CurveDivisor.picClass K D = CurveDivisor.picClass K D') :
    Sheaf.chi (X.divisorSheaf K D) = Sheaf.chi (X.divisorSheaf K D') := by
  obtain ⟨g, hg⟩ := CurveDivisor.exists_divOf_of_picClass_eq K h
  have hD' : D - Scheme.divOf (X ↘ Spec (CommRingCat.of K)) g = D' := by
    rw [← hg]; abel
  have hiso := mulEquivDivisorSheaf K g D
  rw [hD'] at hiso
  exact Sheaf.chi_congr hiso

/-! ## Well-definedness of the degree -/

/-- **Well-definedness of the degree**: Weil divisors of equal Čech Picard class have equal
degree. The class difference is a principal divisor `div g` (extraction `(X)`), and principal
divisors have degree zero (`deg_divOf`, the χ-ledger). -/
theorem deg_eq_deg_of_picClass_eq {D D' : X.CurveDivisor}
    (h : CurveDivisor.picClass K D = CurveDivisor.picClass K D') :
    CurveDivisor.deg K D = CurveDivisor.deg K D' := by
  obtain ⟨g, hg⟩ := CurveDivisor.exists_divOf_of_picClass_eq K h
  have hzero : CurveDivisor.deg K (D - D') = 0 := by
    rw [hg]; exact deg_divOf K g
  have hsub : CurveDivisor.deg K (D - D')
      = CurveDivisor.deg K D - CurveDivisor.deg K D' := by
    rw [sub_eq_add_neg, CurveDivisor.deg_add, CurveDivisor.deg_neg, ← sub_eq_add_neg]
  omega

/-! ## The underlying degree function -/

/-- The underlying function of the degree homomorphism: the degree of any Weil divisor
realizing the class (`CurveDivisor.exists_picClass_eq`). Well-defined by
`deg_eq_deg_of_picClass_eq`; bundled as `classDeg`. -/
private noncomputable def classDegFun (L : X.CechPic) : ℤ :=
  CurveDivisor.deg K (CurveDivisor.exists_picClass_eq K L).choose

omit [Module.Finite K (Sheaf.HModule (X.moduleKSheaf K) 0)]
  [Module.Finite K (Sheaf.HModule (X.moduleKSheaf K) 1)] in
/-- The chosen divisor realizes the class it was picked for. -/
private theorem picClass_classDegFun_choose (L : X.CechPic) :
    CurveDivisor.picClass K (CurveDivisor.exists_picClass_eq K L).choose = L :=
  (CurveDivisor.exists_picClass_eq K L).choose_spec

/-- The degree function evaluates a divisor's own class to its degree. -/
private theorem classDegFun_picClass (D : X.CurveDivisor) :
    classDegFun K (CurveDivisor.picClass K D) = CurveDivisor.deg K D :=
  deg_eq_deg_of_picClass_eq K
    (picClass_classDegFun_choose K (CurveDivisor.picClass K D))

/-- The degree function vanishes on the trivial class. -/
private theorem classDegFun_one : classDegFun K (1 : X.CechPic) = 0 := by
  rw [← CurveDivisor.picClass_zero K, classDegFun_picClass, CurveDivisor.deg_zero]

import AlgebraicJacobian.RiemannRoch.ChiFiniteness
import AlgebraicJacobian.RiemannRoch.MulEquiv

/-!
# The χ-ledger: `chi_step`, `chi_divisorSheaf`, and Riemann–Roch-lite

The Euler-characteristic ledger for divisor sheaves on the curve bundle `X` (integral,
smooth of relative dimension one and quasi-compact over a field `K`, with finite `H⁰` and
`H¹` of the structure sheaf — the two instance hypotheses through which properness enters):

* `AlgebraicGeometry.chi_skyModule`: `χ(sky_x M) = dim_K M` — the skyscraper contribution.
* `AlgebraicGeometry.chi_step` (★ ledger keystone): the one-point dévissage step
  `χ(𝒪(D)) = χ(𝒪(D − x)) + [κ(x) : K]`, from the additivity of `χ` along the dévissage
  short exact sequence `0 → 𝒪(D − x) → 𝒪(D) → sky_x J → 0` and `dim_K J = residueDeg x`.
* `AlgebraicGeometry.chi_divisorSheaf` (★ ledger keystone): the closed ledger
  `χ(𝒪(D)) = χ(𝒪_X) + deg D`, by dévissage induction from `𝒪(0) ≅ 𝒪_X`.
* `AlgebraicGeometry.deg_divOf`: principal divisors have degree zero — transport `χ`
  along the multiplication isomorphism `𝒪(0) ≅ 𝒪(0 − div g)` and cancel in the ledger.
* `AlgebraicGeometry.riemann_inequality` (G9): `deg D + χ(𝒪_X) ≤ h⁰(𝒪(D))`.
* `AlgebraicGeometry.h0_nsmul_point_unbounded` (G9): `h⁰(𝒪(n·x))` is unbounded in `n`,
  for any closed point `x` — no rational point is needed, only `residueDeg x ≥ 1`.

All statements are phrased against the one-point divisor `CurveDivisor.single hx 1`
(definitionally the dévissage twist: `devissageDivisor_eq_sub`).
-/

set_option autoImplicit false

universe u

open CategoryTheory Limits Opposite TopologicalSpace

namespace AlgebraicGeometry

open Scheme

/-! ## The skyscraper contribution -/

section Skyscraper

variable {K : Type u} [CommRing K] {X : Scheme.{u}} [X.Over (Spec (CommRingCat.of K))]

/-- `h⁰` of a skyscraper sheaf is the dimension of its value module. -/
theorem h0_skyModule (x : X) (M : ModuleCat.{u} K) :
    Sheaf.h0 (skyModule x M) = Module.finrank K M :=
  (skyModuleGammaEquiv x M).finrank_eq

/-- **The Euler characteristic of a skyscraper** is the dimension of its value module:
`h¹` vanishes and `h⁰` is computed by `skyModuleGammaEquiv`. -/
theorem chi_skyModule [Nontrivial K] (x : X) (M : ModuleCat.{u} K) :
    Sheaf.chi (skyModule x M) = Module.finrank K M := by
  rw [Sheaf.chi_eq_h0 (skyModule_subsingleton_hModule_one x M), h0_skyModule]

end Skyscraper

/-! ## The ledger -/

section Ledger

variable (K : Type u) [Field K] {X : Scheme.{u}} [X.Over (Spec (CommRingCat.of K))]
  [SmoothOfRelativeDimension 1 (X ↘ Spec (CommRingCat.of K))] [IsIntegral X]
  [QuasiCompact (X ↘ Spec (CommRingCat.of K))]
  [Module.Finite K (Sheaf.HModule (X.moduleKSheaf K) 0)]
  [Module.Finite K (Sheaf.HModule (X.moduleKSheaf K) 1)]

/-- **The dévissage step of the χ-ledger** (★): subtracting a closed point `x` from the
divisor drops the Euler characteristic by the residue degree `[κ(x) : K]`:
`χ(𝒪(D)) = χ(𝒪(D − x)) + residueDeg x`. The divisor `D − CurveDivisor.single hx 1` is
definitionally the dévissage twist `devissageDivisor hx D` of the landed short exact
sequence (`devissageDivisor_eq_sub`). -/
theorem chi_step {x : X} (hx : x ≠ genericPoint X) (D : X.CurveDivisor) :
    Sheaf.chi (X.divisorSheaf K D) =
      Sheaf.chi (X.divisorSheaf K (D - CurveDivisor.single hx 1)) + X.residueDeg K x := by
  have hS := devissageSES_shortExact K hx D
  -- the five finiteness inputs and the `H¹(sky) = 0` input, in the `devissageSES` spelling
  haveI h₁0 : Module.Finite K (Sheaf.HModule (devissageSES K hx D).X₁ 0) :=
    moduleFinite_hModule_divisorSheaf_zero K (devissageDivisor hx D)
  haveI h₁1 : Module.Finite K (Sheaf.HModule (devissageSES K hx D).X₁ 1) :=
    moduleFinite_hModule_divisorSheaf_one K (devissageDivisor hx D)
  haveI h₂0 : Module.Finite K (Sheaf.HModule (devissageSES K hx D).X₂ 0) :=
    moduleFinite_hModule_divisorSheaf_zero K D
  haveI h₂1 : Module.Finite K (Sheaf.HModule (devissageSES K hx D).X₂ 1) :=
    moduleFinite_hModule_divisorSheaf_one K D
  haveI h₃0 : Module.Finite K (Sheaf.HModule (devissageSES K hx D).X₃ 0) :=
    haveI := moduleFinite_jumpModule K hx D
    moduleFinite_hModule_skyModule_zero x (jumpModule K hx D)
  haveI h₃1 : Subsingleton (Sheaf.HModule (devissageSES K hx D).X₃ 1) :=
    skyModule_subsingleton_hModule_one x (jumpModule K hx D)
  have hadd := Sheaf.chi_eq_add_of_shortExact hS
  -- identify the three χ's with their divisor-sheaf/skyscraper spellings (definitional)
  have hX₂ : Sheaf.chi (devissageSES K hx D).X₂ = Sheaf.chi (X.divisorSheaf K D) := rfl
  have hX₁ : Sheaf.chi (devissageSES K hx D).X₁ =
      Sheaf.chi (X.divisorSheaf K (D - CurveDivisor.single hx 1)) := rfl
  have hX₃ : Sheaf.chi (devissageSES K hx D).X₃ = (X.residueDeg K x : ℤ) := by
    have h := chi_skyModule x (jumpModule K hx D)
    rw [finrank_jumpModule K hx D] at h
    exact h
  rw [hX₂, hX₁, hX₃] at hadd
  exact hadd

/-- **The χ-ledger, closed** (★): for every Weil divisor `D` on the curve bundle,
`χ(𝒪(D)) = χ(𝒪_X) + deg D`. Base case `𝒪(0) ≅ 𝒪_X`, step `chi_step`, glue
`CurveDivisor.induction_devissage`. -/
theorem chi_divisorSheaf (D : X.CurveDivisor) :
    Sheaf.chi (X.divisorSheaf K D) =
      Sheaf.chi (X.moduleKSheaf K) + CurveDivisor.deg K D := by
  refine Scheme.CurveDivisor.induction_devissage
    (P := fun D => Sheaf.chi (X.divisorSheaf K D) =
      Sheaf.chi (X.moduleKSheaf K) + CurveDivisor.deg K D)
    ?_ (fun {x} hx D => ?_) D
  · rw [Sheaf.chi_congr (divisorSheafZeroIso K), CurveDivisor.deg_zero, add_zero]
  · rw [devissageDivisor_eq_sub hx D]
    have hstep := chi_step K hx D
    have hdeg := deg_devissageDivisor K hx D
    rw [devissageDivisor_eq_sub hx D] at hdeg
    constructor <;> intro h <;> omega

/-- **Principal divisors have degree zero**: `deg (div g) = 0` for a unit `g` of the
function field. Multiplication by `g` identifies `𝒪(0)` with `𝒪(0 − div g)`
(`mulEquivDivisorSheaf`), so the two sides of the χ-ledger force the degrees to agree. -/
theorem deg_divOf (g : X.functionFieldˣ) :
    CurveDivisor.deg K (Scheme.divOf (X ↘ Spec (CommRingCat.of K)) g) = 0 := by
  have hcongr := Sheaf.chi_congr (mulEquivDivisorSheaf K g (0 : X.CurveDivisor))
  rw [chi_divisorSheaf K (0 : X.CurveDivisor),
    chi_divisorSheaf K ((0 : X.CurveDivisor) - Scheme.divOf (X ↘ Spec (CommRingCat.of K)) g),
    CurveDivisor.deg_zero, zero_sub, CurveDivisor.deg_neg] at hcongr
  omega

/-- **The Riemann inequality** (G9, general conditional form): for every Weil divisor `D`,
`deg D + χ(𝒪_X) ≤ h⁰(𝒪(D))` — from the χ-ledger and `h¹ ≥ 0`. The curve-level
`deg D + 1 − genus` form is derived in `ChiCurve`. -/
theorem riemann_inequality (D : X.CurveDivisor) :
    CurveDivisor.deg K D + Sheaf.chi (X.moduleKSheaf K) ≤
      (Sheaf.h0 (X.divisorSheaf K D) : ℤ) := by
  have h := chi_divisorSheaf K D
  have hchi : Sheaf.chi (X.divisorSheaf K D) ≤ (Sheaf.h0 (X.divisorSheaf K D) : ℤ) := by
    rw [Sheaf.chi]
    omega
  omega

3	description: Build and check Lean in this workspace and read the errors — use Lean LSP MCP for fast proof-writing feedback, then run faithful kernel verification with `lake build` / `lake env lean`.
4	---
5	
6	## Required proof loop
7	
8	Load this skill before editing a Lean file. Before the first proof edit, invoke
9	at least one Lean LSP MCP query for the target (`lean_diagnostic_messages` or
10	`lean_goal`). After every proof edit, invoke diagnostics or the goal query again
11	before starting another tactic attempt. Use `lean_multi_attempt`, hover, and
12	search to investigate candidates instead of repeatedly launching a build.
13	
14	Do not start iterative proof work with `lake build`: it is a slow, final-boundary
15	check. Use LSP for the edit loop and reserve `lake build` for the final session
16	validation (or when a kernel check is specifically needed). When LSP is
17	unavailable or crashes, record that in the report and use the narrowest fallback,
18	usually `lake env lean <file>` or a single module, rather than silently skipping
19	the check.
20	
21	LSP is sufficient between edits and between separate obligations. Do not run a
22	module build after every proof or repeat a narrow build immediately before a
23	configured final build that covers the same files. At the final boundary, run
24	the configured build once and wait for it. Add an earlier narrow kernel check
25	only when LSP failed, the change crosses an interface LSP cannot validate, or a
26	specific elaboration/kernel question must be settled before continuing.
27	
28	- During proof writing, prefer the Lean LSP MCP server for fast local feedback:
29	  inspect goals/diagnostics at the edited location before running a full build.
30	  This is the fastest loop for filling proofs.
31	- Treat LSP feedback as interactive guidance, not final verification. The
32	  faithful check is Lean's kernel via the project build: run the configured
33	  build command, `lake build <Module>`, or `lake env lean <file>` from the
34	  project root.
35	- Prefer the project's configured build command when validating a task. Otherwise
36	  use the narrowest faithful check that covers the changed file/module.
37	- Re-run after each change and repair failures you introduce.
38	- Read errors top-down — the first error often causes the cascade. For each,
39	  note the `file:line`, expected vs actual type, and remaining goal.
40	- A `sorry` left in place is an open obligation, not a success. Do not hide a
41	  hard obligation behind a new `sorry` unless a hint explicitly allows it.
42	
43	## Fast LSP proving loop
44	
45	The `lean-lsp` MCP server gives sub-second feedback — far faster than a build
46	(10–30s+). Drive proofs with it, then confirm with the kernel. Key tools:
47	
48	- `lean_goal(file, line)` — the proof state at a line. Call before writing any
49	  tactic and after each one. Empty `goals_after` = that step closes the goal.
50	- `lean_diagnostic_messages(file)` — instant errors/warnings after every edit
51	  (`[]` = no errors, but *not* proof-complete — confirm with `lean_goal`).
52	- `lean_multi_attempt(file, line, snippets=[...])` — test 3–5 **single-line,
53	  indented** candidate tactics at once and see exactly which close the goal and
54	  why the others fail. The highest-leverage tool for filling a `sorry`.
55	- `lean_hover_info(file, line, col)` — type/signature/docs at an identifier
56	  (point at the first char). `lean_file_outline(file)` — declarations + line
57	  numbers without reading the whole file. `lean_run_code("#eval …")` — quick
58	  standalone `#check`/`#eval`/`#print`.
59	
60	Core loop: `lean_goal` (what to prove) → search a premise (see the `leansearch`
61	skill: `lean_local_search` / `lean_leansearch`) → `lean_multi_attempt` (test
62	candidates) → edit with the winner → `lean_diagnostic_messages` (confirm) →
63	kernel-check the module at the end.
64	
65	## Heavy builds — actually wait for them
66	
67	Read the WHOLE build output, not just pass/fail: warnings (unused variables,
68	deprecations, `sorry` notices, unexpected recompiles) are actionable — fix the
69	ones your change introduced, and record pre-existing/toolchain ones as memory
70	or an inbox issue rather than scrolling past (see the `horizon` skill,
71	"Warnings are work").
72	
73	A cold `lake build` (or one that recompiles Mathlib) can take many minutes. The
74	most common way a session ends on a wrong conclusion is **not waiting for the
75	build to finish**:
76	
77	- Do **not** assume you will be "automatically notified" or "re-invoked" when a
78	  background build completes — whether that happens depends entirely on the
79	  mechanism you used. If unsure, run the build in the **foreground** and block on
80	  it until it exits, then read the exit code.
81	- If you run it in the background, you MUST actively wait: poll its status/output
82	  until there is a definitive exit code (a monitor / until-loop, re-reading the
83	  log), and only then conclude. A background job you started but walked away from
84	  is *not* done.
85	- Scope the build to the narrowest faithful check (`lake build <Module>` or
86	  `lake env lean <file>`) to keep the wait short; reserve the full project build
87	  for final validation.
88	- Never write your final report — or `complete` an inbox item, or mark a task
89	  done — while a build that affects your conclusion is still running. If the
90	  engine cannot wait long enough, say so explicitly under `## Issues` and leave
91	  the next action clear, rather than implying the proof checked.
92	- Before marking a task or roadmap item done/blocked/rejected, add a concise
93	  closing comment with the exact check command, result, relevant files, and any
94	  caveat. If a task has `roadmap_refs`, make sure the linked roadmap items end
95	  with a consistent status and their own sync/closing comment.
96	
97	## When the LSP dies on big import files
98	
99	The Lean LSP loads the full environment for the file you open. On a file whose
100	imports pull in most of Mathlib (a broad `import Mathlib` umbrella, or a module
101	that transitively imports one), that environment is huge and the LSP server can
102	run out of memory or time out and die. This is an LSP limitation, **not** a
103	proof error:
104	
105	- Do not treat an LSP crash/timeout on such a file as a failure of your proof.
106	  Fall back to the kernel check: `lake build <Module>` or `lake env lean <file>`,
107	  which verifies faithfully without holding the whole environment interactively.
108	- Prefer opening the **narrowest** module in the LSP. Avoid pointing the LSP at
109	  umbrella/`import Mathlib`-style files just to get feedback; edit and inspect
110	  the specific module you are proving in instead.
111	- If the LSP has crashed, restart it (or just proceed with `lake build`) rather
112	  than repeatedly reopening the same giant file and getting the same crash.

import Mathlib.RingTheory.PicardGroup
import Mathlib.RingTheory.Nilpotent.Basic

open Module

example (R : Type*) [CommRing R] (M : Type*) [AddCommGroup M] [Module R M]
    [Module.Invertible R M] (m : M) (h : Submodule.span R {m} = ⊤) : Module.Free R M := by
  have hsurj : Function.Surjective (LinearMap.toSpanSingleton R M m) := by
    intro x
    have : x ∈ Submodule.span R ({m} : Set M) := h ▸ Submodule.mem_top
    rw [Submodule.mem_span_singleton] at this
    obtain ⟨r, hr⟩ := this
    exact ⟨r, hr⟩
  have := Module.Invertible.bijective_of_surjective hsurj
  exact Module.Free.of_equiv (LinearEquiv.ofBijective _ this)

example (R : Type*) [CommRing R] (M : Type*) [AddCommGroup M] [Module R M]
    [Module.Invertible R M] (m : M) (h : Submodule.span R {m} = ⊤) : Module.Free R M := by

    obtain ⟨r, hr⟩ := hx
    exact ⟨r, hr⟩
  exact Module.Free.of_equiv
    (LinearEquiv.ofBijective _ (Module.Invertible.bijective_of_surjective hsurj)).symm

2	name: horizon-inbox
3	description: Read and act on the Archon Horizon inbox — list/filter items, understand labels/kinds, comment, archive, create; per-team ownership and read-state; and message other projects or teams via the `horizon inbox` CLI.
4	---
5	
6	The inbox is the durable channel between the human, agent sessions (present and
7	future), and other projects. Act on it through the CLI; never edit inbox files
8	by hand. Prefer `--json` whenever reading command output for exact ids or
9	fields.
10	
11	## Read
12	
13	- `horizon inbox list` — read the inbox. Use `--json` when you need exact ids,
14	  labels, scope, author, audience, timestamps, or comments. Use the list filters
15	  to narrow without losing the overview: `--to horizon`, `--to human`,
16	  `--project P`, repeated `--kind K`, repeated `--label L`,
17	  `--status open`, `--query TEXT`, `--limit N`, and `--comments N`.
18	- In an agent session, an unqualified list means the **open working queue**, not
19	  archived history. It is ordered by attention: required protections first,
20	  unread/direct conversations next, then advisory items. JSON starts with an
21	  `attention` summary so redirecting stderr cannot erase this signal.
22	- `horizon inbox show <id> --json` opens exactly one item and marks it read for
23	  your team. Use `--no-mark-read` for inspection without acknowledgement.
24	- Every inbox command evaluates the full local working set, even when `list` is
25	  filtered. Treat its advisory warnings as a prompt to review duplicates, stale
26	  memories, and consumed notices. The CLI never archives automatically because
27	  only the working agent can decide what is resolved; that agent must make an
28	  explicit cleanup pass before its final report.
29	- Labels are the release gate. Local inbox items default to `agent-ready`, which
30	  means they are visible to agents at run boundaries. Keep that default for
31	  machine-addressed work, and usually keep it for human-addressed notices too:
32	  it helps later agents see that the human has already been notified and avoids
33	  duplicate reports. Use `not-ready`, `rejected`, or no labels only when there is
34	  a concrete reason agents should not see or act on the item yet.
35	- Audience says who should read the item: empty/general, `horizon`, `human`,
36	  `project:<name>`, or a **direct message** to another team: `task:<id>` /
37	  `run:<id>` (older items may carry the legacy `ground` audience). A conversation
38	  may have several recipients; start one with `horizon inbox dm <recipient>...`.
39	  Scope/project says what the item is about.
40	- Horizon reads general items, items addressed to `horizon`, items addressed
41	  to its project, and DMs addressed to its own task/run. It should ignore other
42	  projects' and other teams' addressed items.
43	- A conversation's participants are its recipients **and its initiator**. The
44	  initiator is recorded as `metadata.started_by`; replies become unread for every
45	  other participant, including that initiator. Participants are not ownership:
46	  the initiator remains responsible for deciding when the thread is finished.
47	- Kinds: `conversation` (a direct/group thread requiring prompt acknowledgement),
48	  `hint` (normal guidance), `issue` (problem to fix/report),
49	  `protection` (standing constraint / soft freeze), `info` (a notice for the
50	  human — something you did or noticed they should know, e.g. a renamed project
51	  or an important change; purely informational, never affects what runs),
52	  `memory` (durable agent note or dead end).
53	
54	## Ownership & read-state (your team's inbox)
55	
56	Each running session is a **team**, and the inbox is shared across teams. Two
57	lightweight overlays keep it navigable:
58	
59	- **Ownership** — an item is either *shared with everyone* (the default) or
60	  *owned by one task* (that team's private inbox — e.g. its own memory). Read your
61	  team's inbox with `horizon inbox list --mine` (owned-by-you **plus** shared);
62	  another team's private items don't appear. Own an item to your task with
63	  `horizon inbox add --mine …` (or `--owner <task-id>`), and `horizon inbox own
64	  <id> --mine|--owner <task>|--shared` to move an existing one. Owning your
65	  `--kind memory` notes keeps another team's memory out of your working set.
66	- **Read-state** — read/unread is **per team**, so a shared item several teams see
67	  tracks who has read it. `horizon inbox list --unread` is what *you* have not read
68	  yet; `horizon inbox read <id>` marks it read, and `horizon inbox unread <id>`
69	  puts it back (e.g. you read it but it still needs action). Combine:
70	  `horizon inbox list --mine --unread` is your team's fresh queue — the same signal
71	  the pre-command synchronizer counts for you.
72	
73	Read in this order before editing:
74	
75	1. `horizon inbox list --mine --status open --kind protection --json` — every
76	   active protection is required even if your team previously marked it read.
77	2. `horizon inbox list --mine --unread --kind conversation --json` — open each
78	   result with `inbox show`; reply when a response is needed, otherwise the read
79	   acknowledgement clears it until another participant replies.
80	3. Consult hint/issue/info/memory items as advisory context for the task.
81	
82	The reader/owner id is inferred from your session (your task), so you rarely pass
83	it explicitly.
84	
85	## Act
86	
87	Authorship is automatic: every item and comment you create through the CLI is
88	attributed to your role (normally `horizon`) from the run environment — you do
89	**not** pass `--author` (a stray `--author work-reviewer` is demoted to the
90	`agent` metadata, not used as the author, so the author set stays conventional).
91	If you are a dispatched **subagent**, add `--agent <your-name>` (e.g. `--agent
92	work-reviewer`) to record your identity; it is stored in metadata and shown
93	next to the role in the UI, keeping the author itself a clean role. Items and
94	comments are also auto-tagged with the run/session provenance (a small chip in the
95	UI); you do not pass this yourself.
96	
97	New inbox items use a two-part body:
98	
99	- First paragraph = concise title. Keep it short enough to scan in one UI row
100	  (aim for under ~100 characters); do not put the full explanation here.
101	- Second paragraph and later = non-empty description. Put the evidence, impact,
102	  next action, and relevant ids/files here. The description is **mandatory** — an
103	  item that is only a title is rejected.
104	
105	Write bodies and comments in **Markdown**: the dashboard renders it. Use short
106	paragraphs and `-` bullet lists instead of one wall-of-text paragraph, `**bold**`
107	for the key claim, and backticks for ids, lemma names, files, and code
108	(`` `lem:foo` ``, `` `Foo.lean:42` ``). For a multi-part result, start with a
109	one-sentence conclusion, then use `## Result`, `## Evidence`, `## Impact`, and
110	`## Next action` as applicable; omit empty sections. The CLI rejects long new
111	agent descriptions, opening messages, and comments with no paragraph, heading,
112	or list structure.
113	
114	Do not create an item whose body is only a title. If you need a `[persistent]` or
115	`[temporary]` tag, put it at the start of the title paragraph and keep the rest
116	of that paragraph concise.
117	
118	Before opening a new item, search the open inbox for the same topic using
119	`horizon inbox list --status open --query "key words" --json` and, when relevant,
120	`--project P` / `--to R`. If a live item already covers the same issue, do not
121	open a duplicate: add a comment with the new evidence, or edit the body if the
122	main description is stale. If you discover an open item is obsolete, already
123	solved, consumed, or superseded, add a short comment when the reason is not
124	obvious and then run `horizon inbox archive <id>`.
125	
126	### Conversation lifecycle
127	
128	A conversation is for an expected reply, decision, or active coordination. A
129	one-way handoff or announcement is an `info`/`hint`, not a conversation.
130	
131	1. **Search before starting:** inspect open conversations for the same topic and
132	   participants (`inbox list --status open --kind conversation --query "key words"
133	   --json`). Reply to the existing thread whenever it can carry the update. Do not
134	   open one thread per incremental finding.
135	2. **One question, one thread:** keep follow-ups, answers, corrections, and the
136	   final decision as comments on that thread. Start another only when it has a
137	   genuinely different decision boundary or participant set.
138	3. **Answer before branching:** when a conversation becomes unread, open it and
139	   answer or acknowledge it before starting another conversation with the same
140	   team.
141	4. **The initiator closes:** if `metadata.started_by` is your task/run, you own
142	   the lifecycle. Once the requested answer has arrived and been consumed, add a
143	   short conclusion comment when the outcome is not obvious, then
144	   `horizon inbox archive <id>`. Do this during the session, not only after a
145	   warning says the inbox is full.
146	5. **Do not hide an answer from its initiator:** recipients normally reply and
147	   leave closure to the initiator. For a human-started thread, answer it but leave
148	   it open for the human to consume/archive unless the human explicitly delegates
149	   closure. Use `complete` instead of `archive` only when the concluded thread is
150	   intentionally meant to remain visible in the resolved working record.
151	6. **End-of-session sweep:** before the final report, inspect open conversations
152	   in which your task is `started_by`. Archive every resolved one and state a real
153	   blocker on any that must remain open. An accumulation of open conversations is
154	   unfinished coordination, not harmless history.
155	
156	- `horizon inbox comment <id> --body "..."` — progress note on an item (record
157	  what you did; not to ask the human for clarification). Do not write your name
158	  into the comment body; the author is set automatically. Drop a comment at each **key advance**
159	  while you work an item (a milestone reached, a route ruled out, a blocker hit),
160	  not only at the end — these comments are the item's visible progress trail.
161	- `horizon inbox dm task:<id> [task:<id> ...] --body "Topic\n\nOpening message"`
162	  — start a one-to-one or group conversation. Use `horizon ps` to discover live
163	  teams. Use it only after the lifecycle search above. The sender remains a
164	  participant and owns closure; every reply makes the thread unread for the other
165	  participants. Humans read and reply from the live dashboard.
166	- **Write comments as mathematics, for a human.** State the key step that
167	  succeeded in human-readable mathematical language (LaTeX for formulas), naming
168	  the result and the idea — e.g. "Proved $H^i(X,\mathcal{F})=0$ for $i>\dim X$ by
169	  reducing to the affine case via Čech cohomology." Mention Lean declaration
170	  names and file paths only as supporting detail; the substance is the maths, not
171	  a code changelog. This applies to comments on **roadmap items and tasks** too:
172	  when a key step lands, record it there in the same mathematical, legible style.
173	- `horizon inbox archive <id>` — soft-delete: keep the item for the record but
174	  hide it from the dashboard by default. Use for stale, superseded, consumed, or
175	  no-longer-key context. Keeping the inbox tidy this way is your job (or the
176	  janitor subagent's) — prune memory/info so they remain small.
177	  For a conversation you initiated, this is the normal "discussion finished"
178	  operation after its answer/conclusion has been consumed.
179	- `horizon inbox complete <id>` — mark an item resolved only when it records work
180	  you genuinely concluded and want to keep visible outside the archive. Before
181	  completing, add a short **conclusion comment**: first the mathematical
182	  conclusion (what was proved/established, in words + LaTeX), then concise
183	  metadata (runs, approximate LOC, files/declarations involved). A reader should
184	  grasp the result and how it was concluded without opening the logs.
185	- `horizon inbox add --body "Short title\n\nDescription with details and next action." [--to R] [--project P] [--persistent|--temporary] [--agent <name> if a subagent]`
186	  — open a new item.
187	  - `--to` is the recipient: `horizon`, `human`, `project:<name>`, or a direct
188	    message to another team `task:<id>` / `run:<id>`.
189	    Use `--to project:<name>` to message another project (e.g. "I rewrote your
190	    `foo` declaration more cleanly, you may want it"); use `--to task:<id>` to
191	    message a specific running team.
192	  - `--owner <task-id>` / `--mine` keeps the item in one team's inbox instead of
193	    the shared default.
194	  - `--project` says what the item is ABOUT (its subject).
195	  - `--persistent` / `--temporary` just prepend a `[persistent]` / `[temporary]`
196	    tag to the body.
197	  - `--pending` labels the item `not-ready` instead of the default `agent-ready`,
198	    so it stays invisible to agents until a human releases it.
199	- `horizon inbox add --kind memory --to horizon --body "Short memory title\n\nDurable fact, convention, or dead end."` — record a durable
200	  note / dead end. Memory lives in the inbox, so it is rendered in the "Memory"
201	  section and a human can prune it like any other item.
202	- `horizon inbox protect --body "..." [--project P] [--file F] [--declaration D] [--blueprint-node N]`
203	  — add a semantic standing constraint the Horizon agent must respect (a soft freeze),
204	  e.g. "do not change the signature of `Foo.bar`". These render as a

206	  must be mechanically blocked before dispatch, the user uses the config-backed
207	  `horizon freeze add <file|declaration|blueprint-node> <target>` command instead.
208	
209	Reading convention: an item tagged `[persistent]` is a standing rule — respect
210	it every round and keep it open while relevant. `[temporary]` (or untagged) is
211	one-shot — archive it once consumed. Items in the "Protected" section are never
